content: POLH polymerase, also referred to as DNA polymerase eta, is a protein encoded by the POLH gene in humans. This gene encodes a member of the Y family of specialized DNA polymerases. Unlike other DNA-directed polymerases, it replicates undamaged DNA with lower fidelity. However, it is uniquely capable of accurately replicating DNA that has been damaged by ultraviolet (UV) radiation. Specifically, when UV-induced thymine dimers are present, this polymerase inserts the correct complementary nucleotides into the newly synthesized DNA strand. This process allows the polymerase to bypass the lesion and mitigate the mutagenic effects of UV-induced DNA damage. Additionally, this polymerase is believed to play a role in hypermutation during immunoglobulin class switch recombination. Mutations in the POLH gene are associated with a condition known as xeroderma pigmentosum variant (XP-V). Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by extreme sensitivity to sunlight, progressive deterioration of the skin and eyes, and an increased risk of developing malignant skin cancers at an early age following UV exposure. XP is classified into eight complementation groups, designated XP-A through XP-G and XP-V. Cells from patients in groups XP-A through XP-G exhibit defects in nucleotide excision repair (NER), a critical DNA repair pathway that removes a wide range of structurally diverse lesions, including UV-induced cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (CPDs), (6-4) photoproducts, and certain chemical adducts. The genes and proteins associated with XP groups A, B, C, D, F, and G have been identified and are known to constitute components of the core NER machinery. In contrast, cells from the XP-V group are proficient in NER but exhibit abnormalities in DNA replication. Specifically, these cells demonstrate a reduced ability to elongate nascent DNA strands on UV-irradiated DNA, leading to impaired DNA synthesis under conditions of UV-induced damage.
